messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Discharge Summary:

Patient Information:
Name: [REDACTED]
Age: 52-year-old female
Admission Date: [REDACTED]
Discharge Date: [REDACTED]
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to the hospital due to acute change in mental status, with a history of hypertension, smoking, alcohol dependence, and coronary vascular disease with recent myocardial infarction. An emergency bedside ventriculostomy was performed due to a spontaneous intraventricular hemorrhage. Multiple negative blood, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and urinary cultures were conducted, despite persistent fevers, and she received empiric infections treatment with intravenous levofloxacin and vancomycin.

The patient's neurologic function steadily improved, and the ventriculostomy was discontinued. However, her CSF cultures on day 11 revealed Coagulase-Negative Staphylococcal (CoNS) species, for which she was administered intravenous vancomycin and rifampin.

On day 15, computerized tomography (CT) of the head showed increased intraventricular hemorrhage requiring reinsertion of an external ventriculostomy. Repeated CSF analysis showed elevated white blood cell count with decreased glucose, and CSF cultures yielded CoNS again. Treatment with daptomycin was started, both intravenously and intraventricularly, and the cultures became sterile following 7 days of treatment.

The patient's hospital course was further complicated with respiratory failure requiring tracheostomy and ventilation support, ventilator-associated pneumonia, and sacral pressure ulcer, and Clostridium difficile colitis. 

The patient was successfully discharged on day 65 to a rehabilitation center.

Discharge Medications:
None

Follow-Up Care:
Follow-up appointments with a primary care physician and a neurologist are recommended.

Plan:
Discharge plan: Transfer to a rehabilitation center.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for the admission was a spontaneous intraventricular haemorrhage, which caused the acute change in mental status and needed an emergency ventriculostomy. The CoNS ventriculitis, respiratory failure, pneumonia, pressure ulcer and C. difficile colitis were complications that arose after admission. A non-traumatic intraventricular haemorrhage is coded in chapter I under intracerebral haemorrhage, category I61.

CODE: I61
